replying_to: Replying to Neural Super-Resolution for Mesh-Based Simulations under Scarce Supervision
display_title: Official Review of Submission17149 by Reviewer 3rvZ

summary.value: This paper proposes a super-resolution framework, *SuperMeshNet*. The proposed idea consists of two main components, complementary learning method and inductive bias. The complementary learning employs an auxiliary model and predicts pseudo labels for the unlabeled data. Then, they are used to strengthen the main model's performance. Likewise, the main model generates pseudo labels for the unlabeled data and then the auxiliary model learns from them. This pseudo-label ensembling enhances the quality of pseudo labels and thus improves the semi-supervised super-resolution performance. In addition, subtracting mean of node embeddings from the outputs of MPNN layers turn out to further improve the model accuracy.

strengths.value:
1. I like the idea of employing an auxiliary model and ensembling two models' outputs. It has been well incorporated into an appropriate super-resolution tasks for high-resolution PDE solutions.

2. Application to time-dependent PDEs shown in Section 3.7 strengthens the proposed idea. The visualized results clearly show the performance improvements.

3. Appendix provides rich empirical and visualized results. Also, the real-world applications justify the proposed method's efficacy.

weaknesses.value:
Overall, while the semi-supervised learning mechanism has been wisely incorporated into super-resolution task, I see some critical issues as follows.

1. [**Missing definition of notations**] All notations are defined in appendix, however, it seriously hurts readability. Please bring at least a part of them into the main text to make the manuscript self-contained. 

2. [**Novelty issue**] The authors argue that complementary learning is a novel semi-supervised learning method. However, having an auxiliary model and ensembling two models' outputs in a semi-supervised learning framework is not novel. While it is a wise design of semi-supervised learning framework, it is still a combination of employing auxiliary model and pseudo-label ensemblnig. Recently, the word 'novel' is misused in many paper submissions. I would like to point out that 'novel' means that the proposed idea is entirely 'new' in any aspects.

3. [**Inductive bias substantiation issue**] Inductive bias is not well substantiated. In section 2.3, it is said that "To further improve super-resolution performance, we incorporate two inductive biases into the message passing mechanism of each MPNN layer." The authors' logic is that the accuracy is improved when the mean values are subtracted from the node embeddings and thus global mean is uninformative. I believe this has a serious flaw because the conclusion is based on their own limited observations. The higher accuracy does not explain why focusing on deviation improves the MPNN's accuracy. The same flaw in message-level centering. I strongly recommend better understanding why such standarization improves performance and explain the exact reasons. Otherwise, it makes the whole arguments significantly less convincing.

4. [**Comparison to PINNs**] Recently, PINNs have been widely used to solve PDEs, replacing FEM approaches. What if PINNs are used to directly generate HR images from the corresponding parameter values instead of using GNNs to run super-resolution? Although it may not be exactly within the scope of this study since this work narrows down the scope to 'super-resolution', I think this comparison may be a greatly interesting topic for researchers who study PDEs.

5. [**Poor presentation quality***] Too many important information is missing and appear in the Appendix. E.g., notations, pseudocode of the complementary learning, implementation details of two MPNN models, and many other factors. I understand the space is limited and authors may selectively put some information in the appendix, but too much is missing now. I had to go back and forth constantly to read the paper.

Due to the above limitations, I cannot give a positive score for now.

questions.value: My questions are included in the above weakness section. Please carefully address them.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer 3rvZ, 
We greatly appreciate your time and efforts in reviewing our submission. Below, we have addressed your concerns in detail. We have also uploaded a revised manuscript that reflects the changes made in response to your comments. Please note that the manuscript may be further updated to include additional experimental results conducted during the rebuttal phase, which will be added to the appendix.

### 1. Missing definition of notations
We agree that having essential notations easily accessible in the main text improves readability. Although each notation was originally defined at its first appearance, we understand that the current placement may still force readers to move back and forth between sections. To improve clarity, we have revised the manuscript so that **each subsection now includes the necessary definition of notations at their first appearance within that subsection**. While bringing all notations from the appendix into the main text would indeed maximize readability, the space limitation prevents us from including the full notation table. Nevertheless, we believe that the revision will make the manuscript substantially more self-contained. 

### 2. Novelty issue
We acknowledge your point regarding the use of the overemphasized word “novel,” and we have now **removed all instances of the term from the manuscript**. While the complementary learning itself is not new, we believe that our contribution lies in **applying semi-supervised learning to mesh-based super-resolution**, a domain in which HR training data are significantly more limited than in typical classification or regression problems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that semi-supervised learning leveraging two distinct models aimed to solve two related but complementary tasks can substantially reduce the amount of HR data needed for super-resolution tasks.

### 3. Substantiation issue of inductive biases
We thank the reviewer for requesting clearer justification of the inductive biases. Below, we first discuss why the proposed centering mechanism can act as effective inductive biases, and then present empirical observations that support our interpretation. 

In brief, **centering tends to smooth the loss landscape**, similarly as in the effect reported for batch normalization (Santurkar et al., NeurIPS 2018), which may facilitate optimization. However, because centering removes global mean information, its benefit depends on whether the task of interest relies on such information. To validate this, we have newly carried out a comparative study alongside two different tasks. In our experiments below, we find that centering is indeed beneficial for tasks in which the global mean is relatively unimportant (e.g., super-resolution), but less effective for tasks where the mean level plays a central role (e.g., norm prediction). We now present our results and analyses (refer to Appendix T for the full set of experimental results). Although we report results on Dataset 1, the same qualitative pattern appears on Datasets 2 and 3 as well.

### (1) Effect of the global mean
**Super-resolution**: Appendix T.1 shows that subtracting the mean from LR data leads to only a minor change in RMSE (0.0228 → 0.0235), whereas providing only the global mean significantly degrades RMSE performance (0.0617). This implies that the global mean information contributes relatively little to prediction accuracy. Super-resolution primarily requires learning **high-frequency discrepancies** between LR and HR fields (Y. Guo et al., Theoretical and Applied Mechanics Letters 15 (2025)). Furthermore, our architecture (see Figures 4 and 5) produces HR predictions by refining a $k$NN-interpolated coarse estimate, which may further reduce the reliance on modeling the global mean. 

| Input | RMSE |
|-------|------|
| LR data | 0.0228 |
| Deviation of LR data | 0.0235 |
| Mean of LR data | 0.0617 |

**Norm prediction**: On the other hand, in norm prediction, the global mean appears to contain essential information. When only the mean is provided, performance gets improved, whereas providing only the deviation significantly degrades the performance.

| Input | RMSE |
|-------|------|
| LR data | 0.00269 |
| deviation of LR data | 0.00378 |
| mean of LR data | 0.00149 |

### (2) Loss landscape smoothing 
**Super-resolution**:  We observe that centering makes a smoother loss landscape—qualitatively similar to the phenomenon described for batch normalization (Santurkar et al., NeurIPS 2018). Appendix T.2 shows this effect by showing the smoother landscape obtained when centering is applied.

**Norm prediction**: In this setting, applying centering makes a more rough loss landscape (see Appendix T.2).

### (3) RMSE improvement  
Centering empirically improves RMSE performance in super-resolution, whereas it leads to lower accuracy in the norm prediction:

| Task | Inductive bias | RMSE |
|-------|----------------|------|
| Super-resolution | O |**0.0226** |
| Super-resolution | X | 0.0269 |
| Norm prediction | O | 0.00924 |
| Norm prediction | X | **0.00647** |

Overall, our experiments signify a **task-dependent** effect:  
- For tasks where the global information appears **less important** (e.g., super-resolution), centering tends to smooth the optimization landscape and can improve RMSE performance.  
- For tasks where the global mean is **important** (e.g., norm prediction), centering removes useful information and may make optimization more difficult, leading to degraded performance.
---
### Comparison with batch normalization 
Appendix O compares our centering operation with standard layer normalization techniques. Rather than layer normalization, batch normalization (Santurkar et al., NeurIPS 2018) is conceptually closer to our approach because both subtract the mean across node embeddings. Standard layer normalization, however, additionally includes variance scaling and learnable affine parameters.

Our results (see Table 20) show that **centering alone** outperforms layer normalization and, in several cases, even matches or surpasses batch normalization. This suggests:

- Subtracting the **node-wise mean** (as in batch normalization and our inductive biases) aligns better with the super-resolution objective than subtracting the feature-wise mean (as in layer normalization).
- Additional normalization components (e.g., variance normalization and affine parameters) are not necessarily beneficial for this task.
- **Mean subtraction is the essential component** of effective inductive biases for super-resolution.

We refer to Appendix O of the revised manuscript for detailed results and analyses on this matter.

### 4. Comparison with PINNs
Thank you for raising this interesting point. As summarized in the table below, we have newly provided the performance comparison between PINN and SuperMeshNet. Our results exhibit a clear trade-off. **SuperMeshNet achieves substantially lower RMSE, while PINN attains much lower total computation time per instance**. 

However, these results are not conclusive. Once SuperMeshNet is trained, it can be applied to any new instance without retraining, whereas a PINN must be retrained for every new instance. Thus, when a large number of parameterized PDE instances must be solved, the initial training cost of SuperMeshNet becomes amortized. Likewise, RMSE of PINN can be potentially improved by recent advanced optimization techniques. A more extensive comparison is left for future work.
|Methodology|data preparation time+training time (s)|inference time (s)|RMSE|
|-----------------|------------------------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
|PINN              |5.8                                                   |0.0003             |8.0e-4|
|SuperMeshNet|16467.3                                      |0.0061             |1.0e-4| 

Regarding the experimental setting, we have conducted evaluations on the Poisson equation:

$\nabla^2u=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$,

where $u$ is the solution and $(x, y)$ is the spatial coordinate.

The computational domain is an L-shaped region with six vertices: (0, -0.25), (-0.25, -0.25), (-0.25, 0.25), (0.25, 0.25), (0.25,0), (0,0) and homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions ($u=0$) are applied to all boundaries.

For training SuperMeshNet, we have constructed a dataset consisting of 20 HR and 200 LR samples. The domain is the same L-shape, except that the final vertex is replaced by the variable point ($x_0$,$y_0$), where both $x_0$ and $y_0$ are independently sampled from a uniform distribution on [-0.125, 0.125]. The default mesh sizes for LR and HR meshes are set to 0.04 and 0.01, respectively. However, within the vicinity of the singular point, the mesh is refined by a factor of four for each resolution. On this domain, to generate LR and HR data, we have solved the following Poisson equation:

$\nabla^2u=\sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2}$.

### 5. Presentation quality
We agree that key information should be readily accessible in the main text to improve readability. Following your suggestion, we have made the following revisions:
- Notation: Each section now provides the necessary definition of notations at their first occurrence within each subsection. 
- Pseudocode: Figure 3 in the main text is revised in such a way that it includes a schematic overview of the data sampling, loss calculation, and parameter update pipeline, enabling readers to understand the full process without referring to the pseudocode, which is provided in the appendix.
- kNN interpolation: We added a brief explanation of the kNN interpolation procedure so that readers can understand the relevant part of the main text without referring to the appendix.
- Model architecture: The architectural details of the two MPNN models have been moved from the appendix into the main text. Refer to Section 2.3 in the revised manuscript.
- MPNN implementation details: We have rewritten Section 2.4 in such a way of providing the explanation with a concrete example based on MeshGraphNet (MGN), the most representative MPNN in our experiments.

We believe that these revisions significantly improve the presentation quality and reduce the need for back-and-forth navigation while keeping the manuscript within the required page limit. If you have any further suggestions, we would be happy to reflect them.

**Thank you for acknowledging that most of your concerns have been addressed** and for pointing out the remaining clarification regarding which tasks tend to consider mean information less important.

- Node classification: predictions rely mainly on relational structures, not absolute feature scales.

display_title: Official Review of Submission17149 by Reviewer GW1j

summary.value: The authors aim to improve super resolution predictions to datasets generated from PDEs. Doing so is a promising direction for ML as it can significantly speed up expensive simulations to facilitate faster design processes when the error in accuracy is tolerable. The authors aim to tackle this task by combining two different approaches: subtracting the mean from messages and vertex embeddings, and a semi-supervised training mechanism that resist on predicting the difference between two observables in the same resolution.

strengths.value:
- The authors test this result on a number of datasets, including one with objects. Additionally, although the scope of this work is designed to improve super-resolution with MPNNs, they still compare against other super resolution models and other semi-supervised training methods. In general, I find the number of datasets and the comparisons to other models to be quite good.

- I find the improvements from fully supervised (N=200) to SuperMeshNet to be quite compelling. This comparison shows that SuperMeshNet is able to resolve high resolution images with 10 times less high resolution data, but with 200 low resolution images.

weaknesses.value:
The comparison between fully supervised (N=200) to SuperMeshNet is attributed to two factors, the inductive bias and the semi-supervised training. Crucially, this comparison only indicates that the combination of the biases AND the semi-supervised learning outperforms the fully supervised training. Nowhere in the paper can I find experiments that disentangle the effects of the bias and the effects of the semi-supervised training.

The authors do include a comparison between fully supervised training with the same high resolution images (N=20) as SuperMeshNet. I find this comparison moot as SuperMeshNet is trained with the same 20 high resolution images and 200 more low resolution images. It is well known that adding lower quality data to training can improve results. I imagine if one took any of the GNNs and added two different heads for different resolutions, that would also do better than your fully supervised training results. To me, this test does not provide any information specific to SuperMeshNet, only that more data (even if lower quality) can improve the training results.

I consider an ablation between the inductive bias and the semi-supervised training to be a very important comparison. Specifically, training the benchmark architectures with semi-supervised training (Nh=20, N=200) and fully supervised with the bias for Nh=200, and with Nh=20 and N=200. Without these comparisons, it is unclear what the importance of the inductive bias is, and the importance of the semi-supervised training. That is, given your current results, it is possible that the inductive bias applied to all the MPNNs with Nh=20 and N=20 can outperform the fully supervised N=20 model. If that were the case, then the semi-supervised training would be unnecessary.

Although I find the fully supervised (N=200) comparison with SuperMeshNet to be quite compelling, I consider the missing ablation between the inductive bias and the semi-supervised training to be a severe oversight, as it is unclear if the semi-supervised training is necessary at all. Without justifying the effects of the bias and the training individually, the authors undermine half of the paper (semi-supervised training) making it quite difficult to accept this paper in its current state. If the authors include this ablation study, I am likely to change my rating to some variation of “accept” as I find the final results overall to be compelling, subject to points brought up by other reviewers.

questions.value: - How do the authors think this semi-supervised learning technique would help other architectures? Some experiments applying this learning method to other architectures would be nice to see.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer GW1j,  
Thank you very much for your insightful and constructive feedback. We fully understand your concern regarding the need to separately evaluate the effects of complementary learning (CL) and inductive biases (IB). Below, we present the requested ablation study and clarify their individual and joint contributions.

### 1. Ablation study
To **disentangle the individual contributions** of CL and IB, we have evaluated all four combinations (no CL + no IB (new), CL only, IB only, and CL+IB) under **the same data configuration** (i.e., $N_h$=20, $N$=200). For comparison, the fully supervised baseline has been assumed to use all **200 HR** + 200 LR pairs (i.e., $N_h$= $N$=200). 

| Methodology | IB | CL | $N_h$ |$N$ | RMSE    |
|-------------------|----|----|---------|-------|---------|
| no CL+no IB (original)   | X  | X  | 20     | **20**   | 0.0655 |
| **no CL+no IB (new)**  | X  | X  | 20     | 200   | 0.0454  |
| **CL only**            | X  | O  | 20      | 200   | 0.0269  |
| **IB only**             | O  | X  | 20      | 200    | 0.0371  |
| **CL+IB (SuperMeshNet)**              | O  | O  | 20      | 200   | **0.0226** |
| baseline: fully supervised | X  | X  | **200**     | 200   | 0.0228  |

The results demonstrate that:

- Unlike your concern, both CL and IB indeed contribute to improved performance relative to the case of no CL + no IB (new).
- Both components are necessary for SuperMeshNet to outperform the fully supervised baseline trained with 180 additional HR samples.

Regarding the settings where CL is not used ((i) no CL + no IB (new) and (ii) IB only), you suggested using two heads for each resolution. However, in a standard supervised SR formulation, unpaired LR data without corresponding HR labels cannot directly contribute to the training loss. Since we understand your intention as making full use of all 200 LR samples, we have instead constructed a supervised-style baseline that reflects this idea. Specifically, we (i) have pretrained models to reconstruct LR data from noised LR data (via denoising reconstruction), and (ii) have fine-tuned the models on the 20 paired LR-HR samples. This approach provides a stronger control than the original setting involving training only on the 20 paired samples, as reflected in the lower RMSE (0.0454<0.0655). If you would like to see additional configurations beyond these settings, we are happy to include them as well.

Once again, thank you for suggesting this ablation study. We agree that it provided valuable insights and helped strengthen our work.

### 2. Application to Other Architectures
In our original submission (see Table 4), we have demonstrated that SuperMeshNet is compatible with various MPNN-based architectures (i.e., MPNN-model-agnostic); thus, we have interpreted your question as asking whether our semi-supervised learning technique (CL) can be generalized beyond MPNN architectures. Please let us know if this interpretation is not aligned with your intention.
Additionally, to address this concern, we have applied CL to a CNN-based architecture. Specifically, we have replaced both the LR and HR MPNN processors with ResNet blocks. For regular-grid data, we have also replaced kNN interpolation with bilinear interpolation for computational efficiency. On the regular-grid, time-dependent PDE dataset 2 (see Section 3.1; Table 3; Appendix G.5), CL has been shown to again improve HR-data efficiency and even outperform the fully supervised baseline:

| Methodology                      | $N_h$ | $N$ | RMSE   |
|----------------------------------|---------|-------|---------|
| CL + ResNet                      | 40      | 200   | 0.0339  |
| full supervision + ResNet        | 200     | 200   | 0.0417  |

This indicates that CL is **architecture-agnostic** and can be extended beyond MPNNs. If this new experiment and analysis align with your intention, then we will incorporate them into the revised manuscript.

### 3. Manuscript Revision
The tables presented here will be incorporated into the revised manuscript **after all reviewer responses have been finalized**, ensuring that all requested corrections appear coherently in the final submission.

display_title: Official Review of Submission17149 by Reviewer 5EFa

summary.value: This paper uses a graph neural network to construct a mesh-based, semi-supervised super-resolution framework. The authors use a auxiliary model to obtain pseudo-ground truth for low-resolution/high-resolution data pairs in situations where high-resolution data is missing, thereby enabling semi-supervised learning. They also improve the network's super-resolution performance through node-level and message-level centering.

strengths.value:
1. The authors are the first to discuss a semi-supervised method for mesh super-resolution in considerable detail. This method is beneficial for scenarios where low-resolution data is abundant but paired high-resolution data is scarce, and it has significance for accelerating the training of super-resolution models. 
2. Although the theoretical part of the paper is relatively simple, its presentation is clear. The experimental setup and details are complete and persuasive.

weaknesses.value:
1.	Lack of sufficiently difficult data for the super-resolution task. A major challenge in super-resolution is that low-resolution data often loses important high-frequency details, which can cause significant qualitative differences in the physical field. For example, in the Kolmogorov flow considered in [1], the results predicted by traditional DNS on a low-resolution mesh show very significant differences from the results on a high-resolution mesh after a certain number of time steps (see Fig. 2 A of [1], time step = 1500). However, I do not see such a discrepancy in the results presented in your appendix (Figure 12). This might suggest that for this type of task, low-resolution simulation is sufficient to capture the qualitative details of the physical field we care about, making high-resolution results less necessary. I think you need to add relevant experiments and, following the example of [1], show the simulation data from low- and high-resolution meshes where large differences exist, as well as your experimental results, to prove that your method can also achieve good performance on such difficult tasks. 
2.	Missing comparison of inference times. An important application of super-resolution is to perform simulations on low-resolution meshes and obtain high-resolution results via super-resolution, significantly reducing the time cost of high-resolution numerical simulations. I hope you can compare the time cost of high-resolution numerical simulation with the time cost of (low-resolution simulation + super-resolution) to demonstrate that your method can be used to accelerate numerical simulations. 
3.	Excessive length for content related to a technical trick. Section 2.3 mainly introduces the decentralization of the graph neural network, and the authors emphasize its importance for improving prediction results. While this technique may indeed be important, it is quite empirical and does not deserve so much space in the valuable main text. I hope you can condense this section and shift the paper's focus to the more important presentation of experimental results. You could consider moving some of the figures from the appendix into the main text.

Reference:
[1]: Kochkov, Dmitrii, et al. “Machine Learning–Accelerated Computational Fluid Dynamics.” (2021)

summary.value: In this paper, a neural super-resolution framework is proposed, which supports various message-passing neural networks. A scarce supervision method is designed to relieve the demand for high-resolution data. Node-level centering and message-level centering are applied to enhance the performance and validated by ablation study. Experiments show that the proposed SuperMeshNet outperforms other super-resolution methods and semi-supervised methods while requiring 90% less high-resolution data compared to full supervision.

strengths.value:
- It is in principle reasonable to utilize semi-supervised learning techniques for neural super-resolution tasks, to reduce the demand for expensive high-resolution data.
- The experiments are very solid and various, including the various benchmarks, comparison with full supervision, comparison with other super-resolution baselines, ablation studies, etc.

weaknesses.value: The performance gain is relatively marginal, compared to super-resolution baselines, and semi-supervised regression baselines.

questions.value:
- What are the computational costs for generating low-resolution and high-resolution data respectively in your experiments?
- Will the kNN interpolation module bring computational cost issues?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission17149 by Reviewer iPBS

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer iPBS,

We greatly appreciate your time and effort in reviewing our submission. We fully understand your concerns, and we hope the following responses address them clearly. Note that we have uploaded a revised manuscript, but additional experiments requested by other reviewers are still in progress; we will incorporate all the new results into the appendix and the revised manuscript will be re-uploaded once they are ready.

 ### 1. Marginal Performance Gain
We would like to clarify that the primary **design principle of SuperMeshNet lies in HR data efficiency**, rather than the absolute RMSE improvement. For instance, SuperMeshNet achieves performance comparable to or better than the fully supervised model trained with 200 HR + 200 LR samples, while requiring only 20 HR + 200 LR samples. This corresponds to a **90% reduction in HR supervision** while maintaining or surpassing the accuracy of full supervision. Therefore, while the gain in RMSE may appear marginal at a first glance, the **gain in supervision efficiency—which is the central motivation for semi-supervised super-resolution—is indeed substantial.**

 ### 2. Computational Cost of LR and HR simulations
While simulation costs vary across datasets, the rebuttal period’s time constraints allowed us to measure computational cost only for Dataset 1, as shown below. We can provide results for other datasets later upon request. As shown in the following table, HR simulation becomes dramatically more expensive as the mesh size decreases:
| Mesh size | HR simulation time (ms) | LR simulation time (ms)|  
|---|---| ---|
| 8 | 78.7 |30.8|
 | 4 | 234.7 |41.0|
 | 2 | 949.9 |78.7|
 | 1 | 5437.2 |234.7|

You may wonder about the computational cost of LR and HR simulations, since super-resolution is only meaningful when LR simulation plus super-resolution is faster than HR simulation. Importantly, the combined computational cost of **LR simulation + SuperMeshNet inference** remains significantly lower than that of HR simulation:

| Mesh size | (LR + inference time) / (HR time) × 100 (%) | 
|---|---| 
| 8 | 45.2% |
 | 4 | 19.7% |
 | 2 | 8.9% |
 | 1 | 4.6% |

**As the mesh becomes smaller (i.e., the simulation becomes more computationally demanding), the relative speed-up becomes even more pronounced**. We also refer to Section 3.7 (Figure 7) for graphical visualization.

 
### 3. Computational Cost of $k$NN interpolation
We acknowledge that $k$NN interpolation introduces additional overhead, particularly for very small mesh sizes. As expected, the relative interpolation cost indeed grows as the task difficulty increases, which is investigated below.
| Mesh size | (kNN interpolation time) / (total inference time) | 
|-----------|----------------------------------------------| 
| 8 | 17.0% |
 | 4 | 18.6% |
 | 2 | 29.4% |
 | 1 | 71.2% |

However, even after including $k$NN interpolation, **the total inference cost including the $k$NN interpolation time remains far lower than the case of HR simulation** for all mesh sizes, as indicated in the table provided in Response #2. Thus, while $k$NN interpolation may act as a localized bottleneck (particularly for very small mesh sizes), it does not diminish the substantial overall speed-up achieved by SuperMeshNet. We plan to explore lighter-weight or learned interpolation methods as part of future work.

### 4. Manuscript Revision 
The tables presented here will be incorporated into the revised manuscript **after all reviewer responses have been finalized**, so that every requested correction is reflected coherently in the final submission.

display_title: Official Review of Submission17149 by Reviewer EtFo

summary.value: This paper presents SuperMeshNet, a neural super-resolution framework designed for mesh-based simulations that decreases the reliance on costly high-resolution training data. The approach introduces complementary learning, a semi-supervised method that employs two jointly trained MPNN-based models, along with inductive biases to concentrate on local variations, achieving competitive accuracy with significantly reduced HR supervision.

strengths.value:
1.The semi-supervised complementary learning framework proposed in this paper can achieve accuracy comparable to fully supervised methods with only a very small number of high-resolution samples during the training phase.
2.The proposed framework has proven effective across six different message MPNN types, making it a general solution.
3.The proposed method outperforms the fully supervised baseline with less training data and is faster to train than other semi-supervised methods.

weaknesses.value:
1.Complementary learning requires simultaneously optimizing two MPNNs and performing extra kNN interpolations for every unpaired LR sample, so total training time grows substantially compared with fully-supervised training.
2.Without confidence weighting or external validation in complementary learning, any systematic error in one model is immediately back-propagated into the other, risking synchronized drift that is hard to escape.
3.The mutual supervision mechanism critically depends on kNN interpolation to bridge mesh mismatches, making the entire framework vulnerable to interpolation errors near geometric singularities or sharp gradients.

questions.value:
1.The proposed method demonstrates impressive data efficiency by leveraging only a small fraction of paired HR data. Does the performance vary significantly if a different random 10% is chosen, or if a potentially non-representative set is selected? If there are specific HR selection preferences, how should they be chosen?
2.Both networks share the same encoder although they pursue different output spaces. Could gradient conflict between tasks be reduced by separate encoders or task-specific adapters?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission17149 by Reviewer EtFo

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer EtFo,  
We greatly appreciate your interesting and insightful comments. We provide detailed responses to each point below.

### Weakness 1. Training time
Complementary learning indeed incurs a higher training-time cost compared to the fully supervised baseline. However, the more important factor is **how the overall cost, including data generation cost, scales as the mesh resolution increases**. Although complementary learning adds training overhead to some extent, the reduction in HR data generation time becomes increasingly significant at fine mesh sizes, where HR simulations are extremely expensive. Quantitatively, as shown in the figures in Appendix P, the training time of SuperMeshNet increases, exhibiting a slope of roughly 0.39–0.76, as the mesh size decreases, whereas the reduction in HR data generation time scales much more steeply, with a slope of approximately 1.01–1.24, as the mesh becomes finer.  This indicates that, **once the mesh becomes sufficiently small (and HR data generation becomes correspondingly expensive), the time saved in HR data generation can outweigh the additional training time**, resulting in a net improvement in end-to-end computational efficiency of SuperMeshNet. This regime aligns directly with the primary motivation of our work—accelerating ML-based super-resolution under computationally demanding PDE simulations. For further details, we refer to Appendix P.

### Weakness 2. Risk of synchronized drift
To evaluate optimization stability, we have presented loss curves for five random seeds in Figure 24 (see Appendix R). All runs exhibit a consistent decrease without divergence. Although pseudo-labels may contain potential errors, these errors do not mutually amplify because every training iteration also includes supervision from ground truth HR labels. In other words, ground truth terms anchor both models in complementary learning, preventing reinforcement of erroneous pseudo-label predictions. As a result, complementary learning maintains stable dynamics without synchronized drift. For further details, we refer to Appendix R.

### Weakness 3. Singular point analysis
We have additionally tested the performance of SuperMeshNet on a dataset containing a singular point with a sharp gradient. $k$NN interpolation alone (without ML-based prediction) can be used to predict an HR field by interpolating an LR field from the LR mesh onto the HR mesh. However, as shown in Appendix S, pure $k$NN interpolation produces a pronounced localized error peak at the singularity. On the other hand, **SuperMeshNet mitigates this effect**. Both methods incur their largest errors near the singular point; however, SuperMeshNet shows considerably reduced error magnitude and a smaller spatial region of high error.
Specifically, as shown in Figure 26, it follows that
- Maximum error of pure $k$NN interpolation: 4.18
- Maximum error of SuperMeshNet: 1.57

These results demonstrate that the MPNN in SuperMeshNet effectively mitigates the deficiencies of purely geometric interpolation at singular regions.

comment.value:
### Question 1. HR data sampling
First, the following table shows that selecting different subsets of 10% HR samples introduces a moderate variance: the RMSE standard deviation (STD) is about 6.7% of the mean RMSE and is roughly twice as large as in the “same samples” setting. In the same-samples setting, all five training runs use the same 20 HR samples drawn once from a uniform distribution; in the different-samples setting, each run uses a different set of 20 HR samples independently selected from the same uniform distribution. For both settings, we have measured the resultant RMSE from each training run and have computed the STD across the five RMSE values. 

| Strategy |RMSE mean| RMSE STD|
|-------------------|----|---|
| same random samples | 0.0226 | 0.0007|
| different random samples| 0.0208 |0.0014|

Second, we have found that the distributional mismatch between all 200 LR samples and the selected 20 LR samples—quantified by maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)—strongly correlates with performance, as summarized in the following table. MMD-minimizing greedy sampling (kernel herding) begins by randomly selecting one HR sample from the full set of 200 HR candidates. It then iteratively chooses the corresponding HR counterpart of the next LR sample that yields the greatest reduction in MMD between the LR distribution of the already-selected subset and the full LR distribution, thereby ensuring that the selected HR samples closely represent the overall dataset. In contrast, MMD-maximizing greedy sampling repeatedly selects the next sample that most increases the MMD, intentionally driving the selected subset away from the full distribution.
| Strategy |RMSE| MMD|
|----|---|---|
| same random samples | 0.0226 |0.147|
|MMD-**minimizing** greedy sampling|0.0185|0.058|
|MMD-**maximizing** greedy sampling|0.0259|0.330|

We shall add the above empirical findings and analyses to the appendix of the revised manuscript.

### Question 2. Separate encoder
Using separate encoders apparently improves performance at a substantially higher computational cost, as demonstrated by the following table, indicating that there exists a trade-off between the RMSE and the computational cost.  Thus, we have adopted a shared encoder in the main manuscript in order to reduce the computational cost of complementary learning by more than a factor of three.

| Methodology |RMSE  |training time (s)|
|-------------------|----|---|
| Separate encoders | 0.0192 |962.85|
| Shared encoder | 0.0226 |263.72|

We shall add the above empirical findings and analyses to the appendix of the revised manuscript.

### Manuscript Revision
The tables presented herein will be incorporated into the revised manuscript **after all reviewer responses have been finalized**, ensuring that all requested corrections appear coherently in the final submission.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission17149 by Area Chair Hzsm

summary.value:
The paper presents an interesting semi-supervised super-resolution methodology for reconstructing high resolution (HR) solutions of PDEs from low resolution (LR) inputs. The main result is in significant HR data cost reductions while maintaining similar (and superior) reconstruction errors as full supervision. All reviewers agree that the end result is of high significance.

The main concerns were:
1. Insufficient evidence to show the exact data cost gains
2. Weak presentation of the results
3. Possible easy reconstruction tasks in the experiment suite 
4. Concerns on the experimental protocol and ablation studies

The authors have engaged significantly and added several experiments.

reviewer_concerns.value:
I think most concerns were addressed with some still outstanding. 

1. The new PDE experiment with HR-LR does alleviate concern 3., but is the only experiment with challenging pairs. Further, the results are not fully contextualized - I notice the full supervision reconstruction looks  quite poor, unlike the other experiments where the gains are marginal. There is insufficient discussion in what's happening here. 
2. The authors mention that the central theme is in reduction of data costs but the paper devotes little to explore this. In the rebuttal, the inference times are presented for 1 experiment in the main paper. It does show substantial improvement over collecting more HR samples. However, there is a lot that is unclear. For example, hardware differences in data collection and inference, cost vs accuracy tradeoff is only minimally discussed (Ex: data costs to reach x% accuracy for different datasets with both methods). Given that this is the main contribution, there is only a fair amount of discussion.
3. There is still quite a bit of useful information hidden in the appendix and I had to go back and forth to get the full picture. 

Overall, the paper had a strong methodology with promising results but not comprehensive with regards to the main contribution (reduction in data generation costs) or stress-testing with difficult examples where the LR sample has completely different features. Hence, the paper is still in borderline in my opinion.

reviewer_scores.value: There were several 6s and 4s. Notably, one reviewer increased their score from 2 to 6 given the significant engagement. I believe that all the reviewers may have come to a borderline 5/6.
